TCP is a byte-stream protocol, with no notion of packet boundaries supplied to protocols using its service.  This is why NetBIOS Session Service packets begin with an octet of packet type, an octet of flags, *and* two octets of packet length - so that the packet-oriented NetBIOS-service can provide packet boundaries top TCP.

SMB-over-TCP uses a header similar to that of a NetBIOS Session Message, but with a longer length field, as SMB-over-TCP doesn't need any of the services offered by NetBIOS-over-TCP other than "breaking the byte stream into packets", and thus doesn't need the type and length field bits.

[The current QUIC I-D](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-transport-27) says, in [section 2.2 "Sending and Receiving Data"](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-transport-27#section-2.2):

> Endpoints MUST be able to deliver stream data to an application as an ordered byte-stream.  Delivering an ordered byte-stream requires that an endpoint buffer any data that is received out of order, up to the advertised flow control limit.

...

> Streams are an ordered byte-stream abstraction with no other structure visible to QUIC.  STREAM frame boundaries are not expected to be preserved when data is transmitted, retransmitted after packet loss, or delivered to the application at a receiver.

which sounds as if it offers the same byte-stream service as TCP.

If so, the QUIC dissector should offer similar reassembly services to the ones offered by the byte-stream protocol dissectors for TCP and TLS, and SMB-over-QUIC should use those services.

The QUIC dissector has rudimentary support for reassembly of streams. Subdissectors can request reassembly through the standard `pinfo->desegment_offset` and `pinfo->desegment_len` fields.

You can check the basic HTTP3 dissector (packet-http3.c) for a sample.

> The QUIC dissector has rudimentary support for reassembly of streams. Subdissectors can request reassembly through the standard `pinfo->desegment_offset` and `pinfo->desegment_len` fields.

packet-nbt.c and packet-smb2.c both request reassembly in that fashion, so perhaps they should Just Work.  If they don't, there may be an issue.
@Lekensteyn Thanks, i will look

In my test with the sample capture on the Ask question adding nbss to the quic table worked well, but there was no reassembly required in that capture. It did show something else up in the QUIC dissector though, the stream sub-dissectors are added to the QUIC proto_tree, not the main one. There is some code in the QUIC dissector in process_quic_stream() that tries to move the tree up one level, maybe it needs to go two levels up?

And [this](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/itops-talk-blog/smb-over-quic-files-without-the-vpn/ba-p/1183449) blog post from MS states that QUIC is treated the same as TCP and RDMA for SMB transport purposes which implies to me that we will always see NBSS then SMB.

I think that `protocol` is shown inside the QUIC tree instead of as a top level `protocol` tree is a bug with QUIC and not this patch.

This bug can be fixed in a separate patch.
I agree, it was just noticed when looking at this MR.

it is always the same issue for protocol where it is multiple "stream" on the same packet

May be add a preference ?

I'm not sure about adding a preference, to me it's just inconsistent with every other transport protocol display in Wireshark.

Why would a protocol in a QUIC stream be a sub-dissector of QUIC?
you can have multiple different stream on the same QUIC packet...

I would treat this the same as multiple PDU's in a TCP segment, although that's unlikely to be different protocols.

The packet details would show the protocols in the same order as the data which would imply some hierarchy, but until we resolve the long standing questions about how to display multiple PDU's in the same packet there's nothing much that QUIC can do.
FYI we have the same kind of presentation for other protocols like S1AP, NGAP, etc that can have several streams or sub dissectors called an they are not presented at the top level either.

That said this is because with have S1AP data associated with the sub dissector PDU, and presenting them at the top level of tree would not allow to identify the relationship. This might not be the case for QUIC.

I've never seen those so wasn't aware of that.

IMHO QUIC streams are just a transport and not particularly interesting in their own right, unless you are actually working on QUIC.

In this case as the protocol column says SMB I would expect SMB to be the last protocol shown in the details.

Yes in my specific use case you have more than one protocol in the protocol column (S1AP/EPS-NAS for example).
As QUIC is more like TCP and is really a transport protocol, I agree with you.

>
> Graham Bloice commented on a discussion:
>
> I've never seen those so wasn't aware of that.
>
> IMHO QUIC streams are just a transport and not particularly interesting in their own right, unless you are actually working on QUIC.
>
> In this case as the protocol column says SMB I would expect SMB to be the last protocol shown in the details.

I agree. In this, and most cases, QUIC is just a transport and thus
should not be encapsulating an application protocol in the dissection
tree.
Just like SMB2 over TCP is its own top level protocol and not hidden
inside the TCP tree as "payload protocol" or similar.

There may be places where we want to hide the upper layer inside an
expansion inside QUIC but I think that will be rare.
I think the default should be to show each encapsulated prototol as
its own top level protocol. Make this the default and make the common
case be "new protocol is top level entity".
